ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The trial was prospectively registered on ClinicalTrials.gov on October 29, 2024 (NCT06668532), and approved by the university Research Ethics Board (REB; HE2025-0023).

During the study period, no adverse events attributable to the intervention were reported to the study investigators or Research Ethics Board, and none were identified through review of open-ended responses collected across survey waves.
In this preregistered trial, 1,137 unscreened university students were assigned to 6 weeks of a generative AIpowered mobile intervention ("Flourish") or care as usual.
All participants provided informed consent prior to participation.

A total of 1137 undergraduate students were recruited through a large North American university's Sona research participation system during the summer and fall 2025 academic terms in exchange for research credit.
Participants were required to be at least 18 years old; no other eligibility criteria were applied.

Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio through Qualtrics' built-in randomizer at the end of the baseline survey to either the treatment condition or a care-as-usual control condition in a parallel-group superiority design.

Participants assigned to treatment received access to the Flourish app and were instructed to use it at least twice weekly for 6 weeks; however, research credit was awarded based on survey completion, independent of app engagement.
Participants assigned to the control condition did not receive access to Flourish during the study period and retained access to usual campus or personal mental health resources.
Intervention: The Flourish Platform Participants assigned to the intervention received access to Flourish, a self-guided digital mental health app available on iOS and Android.
All randomized participants were analyzed under an intention-to-treat approach to preserve the benefits of randomization.
A total of 1,137 participants were enrolled in the study between May and November 2025 and randomized to either the treatment condition (n = 556) or care-as-usual (n = 581).
By Week 6, participants assigned to treatment had transcribed an average of 18.9 app-tracked active days (SD = 10.2), exceeding the instructed minimum of twice weekly (12 days total).

Participants assigned to use Flourish twice weekly showed more favorable trajectories across all three outcomes than those assigned to care as usual, with lower perceived stress, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms by Week 6.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Multi-Institutional Study on Student Flourishing
table.existing_data_explanation: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions: Does the use of a digital well-being toolkit (the Flourish app) improve well-being among students over a 6-week period compared to a control group?
table.design_dependent_variables:
Primary outcomes:
Flourishing Scale (Diener et al., 2009), depression (PHQ-2), anxiety (GAD-2), perceived stress (PSS-4; Cohen et al., 1983), affect (Subcomponents of Affect Scale), emotional resilience (Smith et al., 2008)

Secondary outcomes:
Loneliness (UCLA 3-item Loneliness Scale), belonging (Walton & Cohen, 2007; Bollen & Hoyle, 1990), actual and ideal affect (Tsai et al., 2006), expectations and experiences of chatbots (adapted from WAI-SR); trust (Ullman & Malle, 2023), academic self-efficacy (van Zyl et al., 2022), overall school perceptions
table.study_design_overview: Students will be randomly assigned to one of two conditions: 1) the intervention group, where they will have access to the Flourish app, a digital well-being toolkit, and will be instructed to use the app twice a week over the 6-week period, and 2) the control group, where participants will not receive any intervention and will only complete baseline and follow-up assessments during the 6 weeks.
table.statistical_tests: The study will use longitudinal linear mixed-effects models to analyze outcomes across 4 timepoints (baseline, week 2, week 4, and week 6), with institution and participant included as random effects. The primary predictors will be the Time x Condition interaction to assess whether our outcome variables of interest (e.g., emotional resilience) improve more in the Flourish condition compared to the control condition over time.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Participants who fail to complete a minimum of 2 timepoints will be excluded from the final analysis. Additionally, students in the treatment condition who do not use the Flourish app, as well as those in the control condition who gain access to the app will also be excluded.
table.sample_size: The sample size will be determined by the number of students who opt into the study for extra or research credit at each institution, with no minimum set but aiming to collect as many participants as possible.
table.additional_comments:
We will conduct exploratory analyses to examine the association between engagement with the Flourish app and well-being outcomes within the intervention group. We will test whether higher levels of engagement are associated with greater improvements in mental health outcomes.

In addition, we will explore whether engagement levels and the effects of the digital toolkit are moderated by demographic factors such as age, gender, and baseline level of well-being/anxiety/loneliness etc. These analyses will help identify whether the intervention is more effective for specific subgroups over others.

Addressing Question 1: Some data have already been collected (we are a third of the way into the 6-week study) as we needed to launch in alignment with the academic semester schedule. However, we have not accessed or reviewed any of the data.

Additional author: Smaranda Lawrie, Providence College (slawrie@providence.edu)

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

ethics_statements: The trial was prospectively registered on ClinicalTrials.gov on October 29, 2024 (NCT06668532), and approved by the university Research Ethics Board (REB; HE2025-0023).

During the study period, no adverse events attributable to the intervention were reported to the study investigators or Research Ethics Board, and none were identified through review of open-ended responses collected across survey waves.
live_data_statements: In this preregistered trial, 1,137 unscreened university students were assigned to 6 weeks of a generative AIpowered mobile intervention ("Flourish") or care as usual.
All participants provided informed consent prior to participation.

A total of 1137 undergraduate students were recruited through a large North American university's Sona research participation system during the summer and fall 2025 academic terms in exchange for research credit.
Participants were required to be at least 18 years old; no other eligibility criteria were applied.

Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio through Qualtrics' built-in randomizer at the end of the baseline survey to either the treatment condition or a care-as-usual control condition in a parallel-group superiority design.

Participants assigned to treatment received access to the Flourish app and were instructed to use it at least twice weekly for 6 weeks; however, research credit was awarded based on survey completion, independent of app engagement.
Participants assigned to the control condition did not receive access to Flourish during the study period and retained access to usual campus or personal mental health resources.
Intervention: The Flourish Platform Participants assigned to the intervention received access to Flourish, a self-guided digital mental health app available on iOS and Android.
All randomized participants were analyzed under an intention-to-treat approach to preserve the benefits of randomization.
A total of 1,137 participants were enrolled in the study between May and November 2025 and randomized to either the treatment condition (n = 556) or care-as-usual (n = 581).
By Week 6, participants assigned to treatment had transcribed an average of 18.9 app-tracked active days (SD = 10.2), exceeding the instructed minimum of twice weekly (12 days total).

Participants assigned to use Flourish twice weekly showed more favorable trajectories across all three outcomes than those assigned to care as usual, with lower perceived stress, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms by Week 6.

> run_subgroup_lmm <- function(data, outcome, baseline_cat_var) {
>   groups <- levels(data[[baseline_cat_var]])
> 
>   map_dfr(groups, function(group_label) {
>     d <- data |>
>       filter(.data[[baseline_cat_var]] == group_label) |>
>       filter(
>         !is.na(.data[[outcome]]),
>         !is.na(cond),
>         !is.na(time),
>         !is.na(unique_ID),
>         !is.na(term)
>       ) |>
>       mutate(
>         cond = factor(cond, levels = c("Control", "Flourish")),
>         term = factor(term),
>         outcome_z = as.numeric(scale(.data[[outcome]])),
>         time_z = as.numeric(scale(time - 2.5))
>       )
> 
>     contrasts(d$cond) <- cbind(
>       flourish_vs_control = c(-1, 1)
>     )
> 
>     raw_formula <- as.formula(
>       paste0(
>         outcome,
>         " ~ cond * I(time - 2.5) + ",
>         "(1 | unique_ID) + (1 | term)"
>       )
>     )
> 
>     raw_fit <- lmer(
>       raw_formula,
>       data = d,
>       REML = TRUE
>     )
> 
>     raw <- extract_lmer_term(
>       raw_fit,
>       "condflourish_vs_control:I(time - 2.5)"
>     )
> 
>     std_fit <- lmer(
>       outcome_z ~ cond * time_z +
>         (1 | unique_ID) +
>         (1 | term),
>       data = d,
>       REML = TRUE
>     )
> 
>     std <- extract_lmer_term(
>       std_fit,
>       "condflourish_vs_control:time_z"
>     ) |>
>       transmute(
>         beta = b,
>         beta_LL = LL,
>         beta_UL = UL
>       )
> 
>     bind_cols(raw, std) |>
>       mutate(baseline_group = group_label)
>   })
> }

> monotone_observed <- function(x) {

>     if (!is.na(x[i])) {

>     }
>   }
> 
>   out
> }
> max_or_na <- function(x) {

> run_meaningful_change <- function(
>     data,
>     outcome_change_var,
>     baseline_cat_var,
>     elevated_label,
>     missing_nonresponse = FALSE
> ) {
>   
>   d <- data |>
>     filter(.data[[baseline_cat_var]] == elevated_label) |>
>     mutate(cond = factor(cond, levels = c("Control", "Flourish")))
> 
>   if (!missing_nonresponse) {
>     d <- d |>
>       filter(!is.na(.data[[outcome_change_var]])) |>
>       mutate(responder = .data[[outcome_change_var]] >= 2)
>   } else {
>     d <- d |>
>       mutate(
>         responder = !is.na(.data[[outcome_change_var]]) &
>           .data[[outcome_change_var]] >= 2
>       )
>   }
> 
>   responders <- d |>
>     group_by(cond) |>
>     summarise(
>       n = n(),
>       n_responder = sum(responder),
>       pct_responder = 100 * mean(responder),
>       .groups = "drop"
>     )
> 
>   fit <- glm(
>     responder ~ cond,
>     data = d,
>     family = binomial
>   )
> 
>   fit_null <- glm(
>     responder ~ 1,
>     data = d,
>     family = binomial
>   )
> 
>   p <- anova(
>     fit_null,
>     fit,
>     test = "LRT"
>   )$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]
> 
>   flourish_n <- responders |>
>     filter(cond == "Flourish") |>
>     pull(n)
> 
>   flourish_resp <- responders |>
>     filter(cond == "Flourish") |>
>     pull(n_responder)
> 
>   control_n <- responders |>
>     filter(cond == "Control") |>
>     pull(n)
> 
>   control_resp <- responders |>
>     filter(cond == "Control") |>
>     pull(n_responder)
> 
>   flourish_rate <- flourish_resp / flourish_n
>   control_rate <- control_resp / control_n
> 
>   # Risk ratio and 95% CI
>   rr <- flourish_rate / control_rate
> 
>   se_log_rr <- sqrt(

text.text: Randomized evidence for purpose-built generative AI mental health support remains limited.
In this preregistered trial, 1,137 unscreened university students were assigned to 6 weeks of a generative AIpowered mobile intervention ("Flourish") or care as usual.

Across the full sample, Flourish produced more favorable trajectories for perceived stress (β = -0.03, p = 0.010), depressive symptoms (β = -0.03, p = 0.006), and anxiety symptoms (β = -0.04, p = 0.001).

Among participants with lower baseline symptoms, Flourish buffered deterioration; among those with elevated symptoms, improvements were larger with Flourish for depression (d = 1.03 vs 0.56) and anxiety (d = 0.91 vs 0.60), with meaningful improvement in 52.3% vs 31.7% and 50.6% vs 38.1%, respectively.
Reduced perceived stress emerged as a potential pathway to symptom improvement.
To our knowledge, this is the first trial supporting purposebuilt, safety-first generative AI for mental health prevention and early intervention in an unscreened population.
Mental health care is among the largest unmet needs in global health.

Depressive and anxiety disorders accounted for more than 90 million disability-adjusted life-years in 2021, 1 and mental disorders are the leading cause of years lived with disability among young people. 2, 3 A 2025 survey of 135 higher education institutions found that 37% of students screened positive for depression and 32% for anxiety, yet only 60% of symptomatic students received any professional support. 4 This gap extends beyond those who meet symptom thresholds, as many people experience elevated stress, 5 which predicts the onset and worsening of depressive and anxiety symptoms. 6 Perceived stress may therefore represent a proximal, shared pathway to depression, anxiety, and other internalizing psychopathology, making it a broad and early target for intervention.
text.formatted: Depressive and anxiety disorders accounted for more than 90 million disability-adjusted life-years in 2021, <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> and mental disorders are the leading cause of years lived with disability among young people. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> A 2025 survey of 135 higher education institutions found that 37% of students screened positive for depression and 32% for anxiety, yet only 60% of symptomatic students received any professional support. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> This gap extends beyond those who meet symptom thresholds, as many people experience elevated stress, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> which predicts the onset and worsening of depressive and anxiety symptoms. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> Perceived stress may therefore represent a proximal, shared pathway to depression, anxiety, and other internalizing psychopathology, making it a broad and early target for intervention.

text.text: Reaching people upstream, however, requires support beyond traditional care.

Common barriers-time, cost, and a preference to self-manage-limit the accessibility and acceptability of traditional care at the population level. 7, 8 Closing this gap requires accessible, scalable first-line support for stress and emerging mental health symptoms that can reach people, including those who may never seek formal care, before distress escalates to crisis. 9, 10 Young people are already turning to AI for this support.
text.formatted: Common barriers-time, cost, and a preference to self-manage-limit the accessibility and acceptability of traditional care at the population level. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> Closing this gap requires accessible, scalable first-line support for stress and emerging mental health symptoms that can reach people, including those who may never seek formal care, before distress escalates to crisis. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> Young people are already turning to AI for this support.

text.text: Therapy and companionship are among the most common uses of generative AI, 11 and nearly 1 in 5 US adolescents and young adults report using AI chatbots for mental health advice, often without disclosing this use to others. 12, 13 Yet much of this use occurs through general-purpose assistants and companion apps that were not designed for mental health support. 14, 15 These tools can miss suicide risk, 16, 17 respond inappropriately, 18, 19 reinforce maladaptive cognition 20 , or prioritize engagement in ways that are misaligned with user well-being. [21] [22] [23] [24] These risks may be particularly consequential for young people, who may be less able to evaluate the reliability of AIgenerated advice. 25, 26 One prominent model for AI in mental health is an "AI therapist" that emulates a human clinician and delivers treatment. 27, 28 This model promises to scale care without scaling the workforce, but it places AI in a high-stakes clinical role with limited evidence and serious consequences for failure.
text.formatted: Therapy and companionship are among the most common uses of generative AI, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> and nearly 1 in 5 US adolescents and young adults report using AI chatbots for mental health advice, often without disclosing this use to others. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> Yet much of this use occurs through general-purpose assistants and companion apps that were not designed for mental health support. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> These tools can miss suicide risk, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> respond inappropriately, <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> reinforce maladaptive cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> , or prioritize engagement in ways that are misaligned with user well-being. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> These risks may be particularly consequential for young people, who may be less able to evaluate the reliability of AIgenerated advice. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> One prominent model for AI in mental health is an "AI therapist" that emulates a human clinician and delivers treatment. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> This model promises to scale care without scaling the workforce, but it places AI in a high-stakes clinical role with limited evidence and serious consequences for failure.

text.text: In the current study, we tested a different model: AI as a purpose-built, first-line coach that supports emotional awareness, psychoeducation, and structured skill practice.

In this model, AI does not diagnose or replace therapy; it recommends, personalizes, and guides evidence-based support to reach people early and help bridge gaps in existing care, while clinicians provide oversight and quality assurance. 9, 10 Digital interventions continue to represent a primary pathway for increasing access to mental health support.
text.formatted: In this model, AI does not diagnose or replace therapy; it recommends, personalizes, and guides evidence-based support to reach people early and help bridge gaps in existing care, while clinicians provide oversight and quality assurance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> Digital interventions continue to represent a primary pathway for increasing access to mental health support.

text.text: Purpose-built, self-guided interventions are often grounded in evidence-based approaches, can reduce symptoms at scale, [29] [30] [31] and are well established as first-line options within stepped care. 32 However, many struggle to sustain engagement, in part because rigid, predetermined programs cannot readily adapt to users' changing needs. 33 Purpose-built AI can combine the empirical grounding and structure of these interventions with the flexibility, personalization, and conversational engagement of generative AI, dynamically matching evidence-based techniques to individuals' needs in real time [34] [35] [36] [37] while providing guidance, encouragement, and accountability to support engagement and adherence. 38 Realizing these benefits safely requires clinically informed architecture, dedicated safety infrastructure, and mechanisms for human oversight. 8, 28, 39, 40 The Flourish app instantiates this framework through a conversational AI coach ("Sunnie") built on a multi-agent architecture that coordinates input routing, risk detection, evidence-based response generation, structured tools, and clinician review (Fig. 1), together with a closed-loop behavior change design that connects conversational support to skill practice, habit formation, weekly reflection, and goal setting (Supplementary Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Purpose-built, self-guided interventions are often grounded in evidence-based approaches, can reduce symptoms at scale, <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> and are well established as first-line options within stepped care. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> However, many struggle to sustain engagement, in part because rigid, predetermined programs cannot readily adapt to users' changing needs. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> Purpose-built AI can combine the empirical grounding and structure of these interventions with the flexibility, personalization, and conversational engagement of generative AI, dynamically matching evidence-based techniques to individuals' needs in real time <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref> while providing guidance, encouragement, and accountability to support engagement and adherence. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> Realizing these benefits safely requires clinically informed architecture, dedicated safety infrastructure, and mechanisms for human oversight. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40</ref> The Flourish app instantiates this framework through a conversational AI coach ("Sunnie") built on a multi-agent architecture that coordinates input routing, risk detection, evidence-based response generation, structured tools, and clinician review (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), together with a closed-loop behavior change design that connects conversational support to skill practice, habit formation, weekly reflection, and goal setting (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: An earlier version improved several well-being outcomes but did not significantly reduce distress-related outcomes, including perceived stress, depressive symptoms, or anxiety symptoms. 41 The platform has since been expanded to target these outcomes more directly through enhanced psychoeducation, conversational support, and structured skill practice (see intervention and safety details in Supplementary Methods 1). platform.
text.formatted: An earlier version improved several well-being outcomes but did not significantly reduce distress-related outcomes, including perceived stress, depressive symptoms, or anxiety symptoms. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> The platform has since been expanded to target these outcomes more directly through enhanced psychoeducation, conversational support, and structured skill practice (see intervention and safety details in Supplementary Methods 1). platform.

text.text: Note.
The system architecture behind the "Chat with Sunnie" feature in the Flourish app is organized into four color-coded zones: input (blue), safety (red), output (green), and clinician review (gray).

When a user submits a message through the multimodal chat interface, the input is first processed by a router that performs risk detection, intent analysis, event detection, and user preference handling.

If a concerning input is detected, the message is routed to the crisis protocol, which retrieves the user's personal profile, short-term and long-term memory, saved safety plan if available, and relevant local or national crisis resources.
This information is incorporated into the large language model (LLM) prompt to generate a safety-specific response.

If no concerning input is detected, the message is routed to one of several prompt-based conversation workflows grounded in evidence-based techniques, such as motivational interviewing (MI), cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), positive psychology, and social psychology.

These workflows assemble relevant user and conversation context, draw on personalized memory, and send the assembled prompt to a frontier model (GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 at the time of the study) to generate the output.

The output layer then processes the response under explicit guardrails and conditionally calls in-chat tools, presented within the chat, and end-of-chat tools, presented after the chat, as appropriate.
The clinician dashboard presents de-identified session-and user-level data in real time, enabling evaluation of clinical safety, adherence to best practices, and continued iteration on system design.
A real-time alert can be sent to a designated clinician when a situation is classified as an emergency.
Solid arrows denote primary data flow.
PHQ-9 and GAD-7 in-app screening surveys were not available during the study.

Here we report a preregistered randomized clinical trial testing whether Flourish reduces perceived stress, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms over 6 weeks in a general college-student sample recruited without symptom screening.

This population is particularly relevant to prevention and early intervention given its high burden of mental health symptoms, elevated stress, and unmet need for support. 4, 5 To examine whether effects varied by baseline severity, we tested for early-intervention effects among participants with elevated symptoms and for preventive effects, via reduced deterioration, among those with low baseline severity.
text.formatted: This population is particularly relevant to prevention and early intervention given its high burden of mental health symptoms, elevated stress, and unmet need for support. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> To examine whether effects varied by baseline severity, we tested for early-intervention effects among participants with elevated symptoms and for preventive effects, via reduced deterioration, among those with low baseline severity.

text.text: In post hoc analyses, we examined perceived stress as a potential pathway, testing whether treatment-related differences in perceived stress predicted subsequent differences in depressive and anxiety symptoms.
The trial was prospectively registered on ClinicalTrials.gov on October 29, 2024 (NCT06668532), and approved by the university Research Ethics Board (REB; HE2025-0023).
All participants provided informed consent prior to participation.

The primary analysis plan was preregistered separately on AsPredicted (No. 195,084; https://aspredicted.org/yrw2-szwp.pdf), specifying longitudinal linear mixedeffects models with participant and institution as random effects and the condition × time interaction as the primary test.
text.formatted: The primary analysis plan was preregistered separately on AsPredicted (No. 195,084; <ref type="url" target="https://aspredicted.org/yrw2-szwp.pdf">https://aspredicted.org/yrw2-szwp.pdf</ref>), specifying longitudinal linear mixedeffects models with participant and institution as random effects and the condition × time interaction as the primary test.

text.text: As data were collected at a single institution across 2 academic terms, academic term replaced the preregistered institution-level random effect as the clustering variable.
Baseline symptom severity analyses followed the preregistered exploratory plan.
No patients or members of the public were involved in the design, conduct, or reporting of this trial.
Potential adverse events were ascertained through spontaneous reports to study investigators and review of open-ended survey responses (see Supplementary Methods 2 for detailed procedures).

A total of 1137 undergraduate students were recruited through a large North American university's Sona research participation system during the summer and fall 2025 academic terms in exchange for research credit.
Participants were required to be at least 18 years old; no other eligibility criteria were applied.
Sample size was determined by available enrollment in the university research participation system.

Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio through Qualtrics' built-in randomizer at the end of the baseline survey to either the treatment condition or a care-as-usual control condition in a parallel-group superiority design.
Simple randomization was used with no stratification or blocking.

The allocation sequence was computer-generated and implemented automatically by the survey platform; research personnel did not have access to the allocation sequence or to individual condition assignments at any point during the study.

Participants assigned to treatment received access to the Flourish app and were instructed to use it at least twice weekly for 6 weeks; however, research credit was awarded based on survey completion, independent of app engagement.
Participants assigned to the control condition did not receive access to Flourish during the study period and retained access to usual campus or personal mental health resources.
Outcomes were assessed via online surveys at baseline and biweekly across the 6-week study period.
Because access to the app revealed condition assignment, participants could not be masked to treatment allocation.
Intervention: The Flourish Platform Participants assigned to the intervention received access to Flourish, a self-guided digital mental health app available on iOS and Android.

The platform builds on the proactive behavior loop evaluated previously, 41 which connected three components: real-time conversational support from Sunnie, an AI well-being coach; brief, interactive evidence-based activities; and daily and weekly insights that summarized patterns in mood and well-being and fed back into subsequent support.
text.formatted: The platform builds on the proactive behavior loop evaluated previously, <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> which connected three components: real-time conversational support from Sunnie, an AI well-being coach; brief, interactive evidence-based activities; and daily and weekly insights that summarized patterns in mood and well-being and fed back into subsequent support.

text.text: The activity library included established techniques spanning positive psychology, emotion regulation, social connection, and stress management, such as Three Good Things, 42 compliment giving, 43, 44 and paced breathing. 45 Sunnie supported emotional awareness and recommended context-sensitive activities based on users' conversations.
text.formatted: The activity library included established techniques spanning positive psychology, emotion regulation, social connection, and stress management, such as Three Good Things, <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42</ref> compliment giving, <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> and paced breathing. <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45</ref> Sunnie supported emotional awareness and recommended context-sensitive activities based on users' conversations.

text.text: Together, these components formed a personalized feedback loop from awareness to action, reflection, and renewed engagement.
The version evaluated in the present trial substantially extended this foundation to address psychological distress more directly.

Intervention content was expanded with additional evidence-based activities targeting stress and emotion regulation, including progressive muscle relaxation 46 and guided imagery, 47 alongside broader integration of principles from cognitive behavioral therapy, dialectical behavior therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, motivational interviewing, and mindfulness-based stress reduction.
text.formatted: Intervention content was expanded with additional evidence-based activities targeting stress and emotion regulation, including progressive muscle relaxation <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> and guided imagery, <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47</ref> alongside broader integration of principles from cognitive behavioral therapy, dialectical behavior therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, motivational interviewing, and mindfulness-based stress reduction.

text.text: Conversational and safety workflows were also refined through iterative testing.
These changes broadened the predominantly preventive, strengths-based focus of the earlier intervention.
The enhanced platform also integrated support more tightly across components and over time.

Sunnie's longitudinal memory and tool-calling capabilities were substantially expanded, allowing a richer representation of each user's history (including goals, habits, previously used coping strategies and their effectiveness) to inform subsequent conversations and personalized activity recommendations, and enabling Sunnie to select, initiate, and guide structured activities in the moment within conversations.

New longitudinal behavior-change features extended support beyond individual sessions: a habit builder enabled users to translate helpful coping strategies and personally meaningful goals into recurring practices and track them over time, while the Memory Jar enabled users to capture and revisit meaningful experiences and reflections.
The platform also included an enhanced, AI-moderated peer community where users could share reflections and experiences from practicing well-being activities and engage with others' contributions.

Flourish operated under a clinician-developed safety protocol that included automated risk detection, structured safety workflows, AI-guided safety planning, and clinician review of de-identified conversations flagged for potential safety concerns.
See Fig. 1 and Supplementary Methods 1 for additional details on the technical architecture, intervention components, and safety-monitoring workflow.
text.formatted: See Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> and Supplementary Methods 1 for additional details on the technical architecture, intervention components, and safety-monitoring workflow.

text.text: The primary outcomes were perceived stress, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms, assessed at baseline and at Weeks 2, 4, and 6.
All three outcomes were preregistered primary outcomes.
Perceived stress.
Perceived stress was assessed using the 4-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-4), 48, 49 adapted to refer to the preceding 2 weeks.
text.formatted: Perceived stress was assessed using the 4-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-4), <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">49</ref> adapted to refer to the preceding 2 weeks.

text.text: The items assess perceived unpredictability, lack of control, and overwhelm (e.g., "How often have you felt that difficulties were piling up so high that you could not overcome them?").

Items were rated from 0 (never) to 4 (very often); the 2 positively worded items were reverse-scored and all 4 items summed, yielding scores from 0 to 16, with higher scores indicating greater perceived stress.
Internal consistency across waves ranged from α = .69 to .74.

Depressive symptoms were assessed using the 2-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-2), 50 which assesses depressed mood and anhedonia over the preceding 2 weeks (e.g., "Little interest or pleasure in doing things").
text.formatted: Depressive symptoms were assessed using the 2-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-2), <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50</ref> which assesses depressed mood and anhedonia over the preceding 2 weeks (e.g., "Little interest or pleasure in doing things").

text.text: Items were rated from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day) and summed, yielding scores from 0 to 6, with higher scores indicating greater depressive symptom severity.
Internal consistency across waves ranged from α = .66 to .75.

Anxiety symptoms were assessed using the 2-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-2), 51 which assesses anxiety and uncontrollable worry over the preceding 2 weeks (e.g., "Feeling nervous, anxious or on edge").
text.formatted: Anxiety symptoms were assessed using the 2-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-2), <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51</ref> which assesses anxiety and uncontrollable worry over the preceding 2 weeks (e.g., "Feeling nervous, anxious or on edge").

text.text: Items were rated from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day) and summed, yielding scores from 0 to 6, with higher scores indicating greater anxiety symptom severity.
Internal consistency across waves ranged from α = .81 to .86.
Primary analyses used linear mixed-effects models in R, fit using the lme4 52 and lmerTest 53 packages to estimate trajectories for stress, as well as depression and anxiety symptoms over time.
text.formatted: Primary analyses used linear mixed-effects models in R, fit using the lme4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref> and lmerTest <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> packages to estimate trajectories for stress, as well as depression and anxiety symptoms over time.

text.text: Standardized coefficients and effect sizes were computed using the parameters 54 and effectsize 55 packages, respectively.
text.formatted: Standardized coefficients and effect sizes were computed using the parameters <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54</ref> and effectsize <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> packages, respectively.

text.text: For each outcome, models included fixed effects of condition, time, and the condition × time interaction, with random intercepts for participant and academic term.
Time was zero-centered, with the 4 assessment waves (baseline, Week 2, Week 4, and Week 6) coded as -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, and 1.5, respectively.
The condition × time interaction served as the primary test of intervention effects.
All randomized participants were analyzed under an intention-to-treat approach to preserve the benefits of randomization.
Mixedeffects models included all available outcome data under a missing-at-random assumption (see Supplementary Note 3 for attrition and missingness checks).

Although the preregistered exclusion criteria were not applied in primary analyses to retain the full randomized sample, sensitivity analyses showed that results were robust when these criteria were applied (see Supplementary Note 1).

Post hoc sensitivity analyses additionally adjusted for baseline socioeconomic status as a five-category variable, with academic term treated as a fixed effect and a participant-level random intercept (Supplementary Note 2).
All statistical tests were two-sided where applicable, with significance evaluated at α = .05.
Unless otherwise noted, p values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons; Bonferroni corrections were applied to exploratory demographic moderation and engagement analyses (Supplementary Note 5).

To examine whether intervention effects varied across baseline severity, we tested whether benefits were concentrated among participants with elevated symptoms, consistent with an early intervention effect, or also extended to participants with low baseline severity through reduced deterioration relative to control, consistent with a broader preventive effect.
We categorized participants separately for each outcome.

Depressive and anxiety symptoms were classified as low (<3) or elevated (≥3) using established PHQ-2 and GAD-2 screening thresholds. 56 For perceived stress, for which no validated cutoff exists, we used the scale midpoint to classify participants as having lower (PSS-4 <8) or higher (PSS-4 ≥8) baseline stress.
text.formatted: Depressive and anxiety symptoms were classified as low (<3) or elevated (≥3) using established PHQ-2 and GAD-2 screening thresholds. <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">56</ref> For perceived stress, for which no validated cutoff exists, we used the scale midpoint to classify participants as having lower (PSS-4 <8) or higher (PSS-4 ≥8) baseline stress.

text.text: We then fit full interaction models of condition, time, and baseline-severity group, with the condition × time × baseline-severity interaction serving as the formal test of moderation.

To aid interpretation, we also examined trajectories within baseline-severity strata for each outcome. important differences (MIDs) of 5 points for the PHQ-9 57 and 4 points for the GAD-7 58 and thus representing a conservative proxy for clinically meaningful change on the full-length scales.
text.formatted: To aid interpretation, we also examined trajectories within baseline-severity strata for each outcome. important differences (MIDs) of 5 points for the PHQ-9 <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57</ref> and 4 points for the GAD-7 <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58</ref> and thus representing a conservative proxy for clinically meaningful change on the full-length scales.

text.text: These analyses used chi-square tests, risk ratios, absolute risk reduction, and number needed to treat (NNT = 1/ARR).

To examine perceived stress as a potential pathway linking the intervention to subsequent changes in depressive and anxiety symptoms, we conducted a post hoc random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) 59 using the lavaan package 60 in R. The model jointly included perceived stress, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms at baseline and Weeks 2, 4, and 6.

text.text: Repeated measures of each outcome were decomposed into a stable between-person random intercept and wave-specific within-person components, allowing stable between-person differences and their covariation to be separated from within-person deviations over time.
Random intercepts were allowed to covary.

At the within-person level, adjacent-wave autoregressive and reciprocal cross-lagged paths were estimated simultaneously, along with within-wave residual covariances to account for occasion-specific shared variance, including related item content across measures.

Corresponding autoregressive and cross-lagged paths were initially freely estimated across intervals and subsequently constrained to equality; the stationary model was retained if these constraints did not worsen model fit.

Treatment condition predicted the within-person components at each postbaseline wave, with these paths freely estimated across waves, and academic term was included as a covariate predicting within-person components at all waves.
The model was estimated using robust maximum likelihood (MLR), with full-information maximum likelihood for missing data.

Overall model fit was evaluated using the robust comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis index (TLI), root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR).
Nested models were compared using a robust scaled χ² difference test.
The focal indirect effects tested the temporal sequence from treatment through Week 4 perceived stress to Week 6 depressive and anxiety symptoms.

For inference on the focal indirect effects, the stationary model was reestimated using maximum likelihood (ML) with 5,000 nonparametric bootstrap resamples and percentile 95% confidence intervals; point estimates were identical to those from the corresponding MLR fit.

Week 2 and serial stress pathways, as well as reciprocal symptom-to-stress pathways, were also examined.

Two sensitivity analyses assessed robustness to alternative longitudinal specifications: an RI-CLPM allowing treatment to predict the random intercepts and a conventional cross-lagged panel model using observed scores.
Technical specifications and full estimates are reported in Supplementary Note 7.

Across outcomes, the descriptive pattern was therefore one of less deterioration among participants with lower baseline severity and greater improvement among participants with higher baseline severity.

Because baseline severity did not significantly moderate intervention effects, these patterns should not be interpreted as evidence that treatment effects differed statistically between severity groups.
We separately examined meaningful improvement in depressive symptoms among participants with elevated PHQ-2 scores (≥3) and in anxiety symptoms among those with elevated GAD-2 scores (≥ 3).

To our knowledge, this is the first randomized trial in an unscreened general population testing a purposebuilt generative AI platform as first-line support spanning prevention and early intervention for perceived stress, depression, and anxiety.

Participants assigned to use Flourish twice weekly showed more favorable trajectories across all three outcomes than those assigned to care as usual, with lower perceived stress, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms by Week 6.

Benefits were observed across baseline severity: among participants with low baseline severity, Flourish reduced deterioration relative to control, consistent with a broader preventive effect; among those with elevated severity, Flourish produced greater improvement, consistent with an early intervention effect.
Among participants with elevated depressive and anxiety symptoms, Flourish also increased rates of meaningful symptom improvement for depressive symptoms (RR = 1.65) and anxiety symptoms (RR = 1.33).

These findings extend prior work showing that app-and chatbot-based interventions can reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety. 27, 29, 30 The trial also points to perceived stress as a potential pathway to broader symptom improvement.

Flourish combines emotional awareness, conversational coping support, structured skills, and action planning, which may help users experience demands as more manageable and reduce progression from stress to broader symptoms.
The overall pattern is consistent with a broadly deployable first-line support model combining scalable, self-guided access with clinician oversight.

For individuals with lower baseline severity, such support may help prevent deterioration during demanding periods and during a developmental window when many psychiatric conditions first emerge. 62 For those already experiencing elevated distress, greater symptom reductions and higher rates of meaningful improvement suggest potential value as an early intervention resource.
text.formatted: For individuals with lower baseline severity, such support may help prevent deterioration during demanding periods and during a developmental window when many psychiatric conditions first emerge. <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62</ref> For those already experiencing elevated distress, greater symptom reductions and higher rates of meaningful improvement suggest potential value as an early intervention resource.

text.text: This dual benefit aligns with the dynamic nature of psychological distress, which fluctuates along a continuum and may benefit from support spanning stress management, prevention, and early intervention.

The present findings also differ from an earlier preregistered randomized trial of Flourish 41 , which improved well-being-related outcomes but did not significantly reduce perceived stress, depressive symptoms, or anxiety symptoms.
text.formatted: The present findings also differ from an earlier preregistered randomized trial of Flourish <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> , which improved well-being-related outcomes but did not significantly reduce perceived stress, depressive symptoms, or anxiety symptoms.

text.text: The current trial evaluated an expanded platform with a more advanced AI architecture designed to provide more personalized and targeted support for psychological distress and found significant effects across all three outcomes.

Although the contributions of individual platform features remain to be tested, the contrasting findings suggest that AI mental health platforms may benefit from integrating multiple evidence-based strategies rather than relying on a single intervention framework.
Several limitations warrant consideration.
First, the care-as-usual control condition limits conclusions about whether effects were attributable to Flourish-specific features rather than nonspecific factors such as attention or expectation.

Second, depression and anxiety were assessed using the PHQ-2 and GAD-2, which are well-validated screening measures but not diagnostic instruments, limiting inferences about effects on formally diagnosed disorders.
Third, this trial focused on young adults and included a predominantly female sample.

Although this population is particularly relevant given the elevated burden of depression and anxiety in young adulthood, 63 especially among women, 64, 65 the sample composition may limit generalizability to other populations.
text.formatted: Although this population is particularly relevant given the elevated burden of depression and anxiety in young adulthood, <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">63</ref> especially among women, <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">65</ref> the sample composition may limit generalizability to other populations.

text.text: Fourth, the 6-week duration limits conclusions about durability.
Fifth, the mixed-effects analyses and RI-CLPM estimation using FIML assumed that data were missing at random; although attrition was similar across conditions, this assumption cannot be verified.

text.text: The focal indirect effects were consistent with an indirect pathway from treatment through lower perceived stress at Week 4 to lower depressive symptoms at Week 6 (indirect effect = -0.027; 95% percentile bootstrap CI [-0.056, -0.004]) and lower anxiety symptoms at Week 6 (-0.018; 95% CI [-0.044, -0.0003]).
Earlier Week 2 and serial stress pathways had confidence intervals that included zero (Supplementary Note 7).

Across two sensitivity analyses, the focal indirect effects remained negative; confidence intervals excluded zero in the conventional CLPM and narrowly included zero when treatment was additionally allowed to predict the RI-CLPM random intercepts (Supplementary Note 7).
Sixth, concurrent psychotherapy and medication use were not recorded, limiting characterization of the care context and comparison of standalone versus adjunctive use.
Finally, the stress pathway analyses were post hoc.

Although random-intercept decomposition estimates within-person indirect effects net of stable between-person differences, it cannot exclude time-varying confounding of the stress-symptom association (e.g., sleep or behavioral activation); use of brief observed composites and conceptual overlap among stress, depression, and anxiety may also complicate interpretation of cross-lagged associations.These analyses support perceived stress as a potential mechanism but do not establish a causal stresssymptom pathway.Future research should examine the durability and generalizability of symptom improvements and identify which interventions work best for whom and when, including through just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs).
Future studies should also causally test the stress-symptom pathway, using approaches such as denser longitudinal assessments and experimental manipulation of stress-focused components.

At the health-system level, beyond standalone self-guided use, purpose-built AI should be evaluated within stepped-care, blended-care, and therapy-companion models,66 including whether benefits persist or increase when AI complements ongoing treatment and how such systems can flexibly support individuals before, during, and after clinical care.Together, these findings provide randomized evidence that a purpose-built, clinician-overseen AI platform can improve trajectories of perceived stress, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms in an unscreened population, across levels of baseline severity.

By combining the evidence base and structure of self-guided digital interventions with the flexibility and engagement of conversational AI, such platforms may offer scalable first-line support spanning prevention and early intervention.
